content: The guideline emphasizes the importance of involving a diverse group of stakeholders, both within and outside the health sector, to ensure effective implementation. This includes researchers, civil society organizations, representatives of underserved communities, healthcare workers, policymakers, donors, and advocates. Such interdisciplinary collaboration is critical to addressing the multifaceted challenges in healthcare delivery. The anticipated impact of the guideline is significant, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, where effective implementation will likely necessitate a reorganization of care systems and redistribution of healthcare resources. This may involve the development of tools such as client cards and registers to document and monitor recommended practices, the establishment of supportive laws and policies, and the reallocation of financial resources to address existing gaps. Given the potential barriers to implementation, a phased approach to adopting, adapting, and operationalizing the guideline recommendations may be required. The World Health Organization (WHO) is prepared to support countries in overcoming these barriers by providing strategies to operationalize the people-centered approach and key principles underpinning the guideline. In February 2021, WHO introduced the first SMART guideline, which stands for standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable. This innovative approach aims to systematize and accelerate the consistent application of recommendations in the digital age. By leveraging interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, and technical specifications, SMART guidelines transform the adaptation and implementation process, ensuring fidelity and expediting uptake. The SMART framework provides a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even in countries that are not fully digital. Monitoring and evaluation systems are essential to assess the impact of the guideline. These systems must be practical, straightforward, and capable of collecting current and actionable information. The implementation and impact of the recommendations will be monitored at various levels, including health service, regional, and national levels, using existing indicators. However, given the private nature of many self-care practices, alternative methods to evaluate the impact of interventions must be developed. Emphasis on uptake and use by underserved populations necessitates meaningful engagement with affected communities. WHO, in collaboration with its Department of Health Metrics and Measurement, will monitor and evaluate countryand regional-level data on health-seeking behaviors and the implementation of selected self-care interventions. This data will provide insights into the shortto medium-term impact of self-care interventions on national policies across WHO Member States. The WHO Thirteenth General Programme of Work Impact Framework will also be utilized to monitor these interventions. The guideline employs a living guideline approach, hosted on the interactive MAGICapp platform, linked to the WHO self-care interventions health topic website. All research evidence and references are accessible on the web platform and available for download. Updates to recommendations will be clearly labeled with the date of the most recent update, and updated PDF versions will be made available on the WHO website to ensure accessibility in areas with unreliable internet access. A feedback option will also be provided to allow users to suggest updates or clarifications. Future updates to the guideline will include additional topics, recommendations, good practice statements, and considerations relevant to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR). These may address areas such as menstrual hygiene, pain control for dysmenorrhea, hormone therapy for menopausal disorders, vaginal pessaries for pelvic organ prolapse, and noncommunicable diseases. Emerging evidence on communicable diseases, such as the self-use of the dapivirine vaginal ring for HIV prevention and malaria bed nets, will also be incorporated. The guideline will be updated as new evidence becomes available, following the GREAT Network framework, which systematically identifies and addresses evidence gaps. The rapidly evolving nature of self-care interventions necessitates continuous literature review and the development of new recommendations based on emerging evidence. The WHO Guideline Steering Group will monitor research developments in self-care interventions and collaborate with other relevant departments to expand the scope to additional health topics. All technical products developed during the guideline's creation, including systematic review reports, search strategies, and dates, will be archived for future reference. Concerns about the validity of recommendations based on new evidence will prompt systematic review updates, using the original search strategy. New questions identified during scoping exercises will undergo evidence retrieval, synthesis, and application of the GRADE approach, in line with WHO standards for guideline development. WHO aims to develop further guidance that promotes equity, feasibility, and improvements in self-care, ensuring that appropriate recommendations are included in future guideline versions. These recommendations will be designed for adoption and implementation by countries and programs, contributing to better health outcomes globally.
